newsitem.title: USA: Higher breast cancer risk for some Jews - study.
newsitem.headline: Higher breast cancer risk for some Jews - study.

text.p: Jewish women of East European ancestry who carry a particular genetic mutation may have a much higher than average risk of getting breast cancer, a new study reported on Wednesday.

But scientists at the National Cancer Institute who conducted the study had no specific advice for these women on whether they should be tested for the mutation or what they should do if they have it.

"Basically, we really don't know what to tell women," said Dr. Margaret Tucker, one of the study's authors. "We really don't know what the co-factors are that explain why some women have a very high risk of developing breast cancer early."

However, Tucker noted that among those studied, there were five women over 70 who had the mutation who never got cancer, and there was currently no way to predict which women with the genetic mutation would get the disease.

Tucker also stressed that mutations in the two genes known to be associated with breast, ovarian and prostate cancer -- genes known as BRCA1 and BRCA2 -- account for only 7 percent of breast cancer in Jewish women.

Another author, Dr. Jeffrey Struewing, acknowledged that there was concern about increasing anxiety among Ashkenazi Jews, those of East and Central European ancestry who account for about 90 percent of the American Jewish population.
"It could increase alarm but I think that our estimate of cancer is lower than the previous ones so I would think that it might lower the anxiety," Struewing said.

The study, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, found that among Ashkenazi Jews who carry the mutation, women have a 56 percent chance of getting breast cancer by age 70, or more than four times the percentage for women without the mutated gene.
This was substantially less than the 76 percent to 87 percent percent chance that scientists had previously estimated for those with the genetic alteration, the scientists said at a news conference.
The average American woman has a 7-8 percent risk of getting breast cancer by age 70, the institute said.
The breast cancer genes were isolated in 1994 and 1995.

"I think the issue is not whether a Jewish person should be tested or not but what information do we have to date, which is more than we had two weeks ago," Caryn Lerman of Georgetown University Medical Centre said. "Some people may decide for themselves that they do not wish to know because there's too much uncertainty."

Arguments against getting tested for the mutation include the imperfect screening and treatment options available and possible discrimination in health insurance for those who test positive, Lerman said.
The scientists acknowledged one possible course of action for those shown to be at higher risk for breast cancer is prophylactic mastectomy, the removal of healthy breast tissue.
The institute's scientists had no position on this, saying it was a personal decision, although Struewing noted that preliminary studies estimate that such mastectomies may be 90 percent protective.
However, in a special report in the New England Journal, four doctors wrote that prophylactic surgery "provides substantial gains in life expectancy."

The institute's scientists reached their findings by taking blood samples from 5,318 volunteers from the Ashkenazi Jewish population in the Washington D.C. area, after early studies showed a higher incidence of mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 among Ashkenazi Jews with family histories of cancer.
